etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English amyable, from Old French amiable, from Late Latin amīcābilis (“friendly”), from Latin amīcus (“friend”), from amō (“love”, verb). The meaning has been influenced by French amiable and Latin amābilis (“loveable”) (whence English aimable and amable). Doublet of amicable. Compare with amorous, amability.

quote.citation: 1777, Richard Brinsley Sheridan, The School for Scandal, V.i:
quote.text: The sums I have lent him! indeed—I have been exceedingly to blame—it was an amiable weakness!

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter III, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: A short time afterward at the opera Gerald dragged him into a parterre to say something amiable to one of the amiable débutante Craig girls—and Selwyn found himself again facing Alixe.

definitions.definition: Of a pleasant and likeable nature; kind-hearted; easy to like
